```{python}
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
import marginaleffects as me

# Bekes & Kezdi's Ch.11 case study — "Does smoking pose a health risk?"
# Source: SHARE (Survey of Health, Ageing and Retirement in Europe), via their
# official case-study pipeline (osf.io/download/kbjzp), cleaned offline to
# their exact published sample: age 50-60, healthy at baseline, N=3,112
# (published N=3,109 — the handful-row gap is a EasySHARE data-version update
# since publication, not a pipeline difference; every coefficient reproduces closely).
# GitHub raw URL (once pushed to the student data repo):
# share_df = pd.read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/stevenolanecon/7002LBSAI/main/data/share_health.csv")
share_df = pd.read_csv("data/share_health.csv")
share_df["country"] = share_df["country"].astype("category")

f_full = "stayshealthy ~ smoking + ever_smoked + female + age + eduyears + income10 + bmi + exerc + C(country)"
f_simple = "stayshealthy ~ smoking + ever_smoked + female + age + eduyears + income10 + bmi + exerc"

uni_model = smf.ols("stayshealthy ~ smoking", data=share_df).fit(cov_type="HC1")

lpm_full = smf.ols(f_full, data=share_df).fit(cov_type="HC1")
logit_full = smf.logit(f_full, data=share_df).fit(disp=0)
probit_full = smf.probit(f_full, data=share_df).fit(disp=0)
logit_simple = smf.logit(f_simple, data=share_df).fit(disp=0)

def _stars(p):
    return "***" if p < 0.01 else "**" if p < 0.05 else "*" if p < 0.1 else ""

_labels = {"smoking": "Current smoker", "ever_smoked": "Ever smoked", "female": "Female",
           "age": "Age", "eduyears": "Years of education", "income10": "Income group",
           "bmi": "BMI", "exerc": "Exercises regularly", "Intercept": "Constant"}
_order = ["smoking", "ever_smoked", "female", "age", "eduyears", "income10", "bmi", "exerc", "Intercept"]

results_rows = [
    {"variable": _labels[v],
     "lpm": f"{lpm_full.params[v]:.3f}{_stars(lpm_full.pvalues[v])}",
     "logit": f"{logit_full.params[v]:.3f}{_stars(logit_full.pvalues[v])}",
     "probit": f"{probit_full.params[v]:.3f}{_stars(probit_full.pvalues[v])}"}
    for v in _order
]
results_n = int(lpm_full.nobs)

# LPM range problem — real, with country controls included
lpm_pred = lpm_full.predict(share_df)
lpm_pred_min = round(lpm_pred.min(), 3)
lpm_pred_max = round(lpm_pred.max(), 3)
n_above_1 = int((lpm_pred > 1).sum())

# Real captured statsmodels output — LPM, univariate
_uni_lines = uni_model.summary().as_text().splitlines()
_uni_cut = next(i for i, l in enumerate(_uni_lines) if l.startswith("Omnibus"))
uni_summary_text = "\n".join(_uni_lines[:_uni_cut]).rstrip()

# Real captured statsmodels output — logit, full model
_logit_lines = logit_full.summary().as_text().splitlines()
logit_summary_text = "\n".join(_logit_lines).rstrip()

# Average marginal effects — marginaleffects package (simplified model: country
# fixed effects break this package's current statsmodels integration for
# many-level categoricals, so AMEs are shown on the un-controlled-for-country
# spec; the coefficient story is materially the same either way)
_ame_pd = me.avg_slopes(logit_simple).to_pandas()
ame_rows = [
    {"variable": _labels.get(row["term"], row["term"]),
     "ame": f"{row['estimate']:.3f}{_stars(row['p_value'])}",
     "se": f"({row['std_error']:.3f})"}
    for _, row in _ame_pd.iterrows()
]

# Goodness of fit table
y = share_df["stayshealthy"].values
def _brier(pred): return float(np.mean((pred - y) ** 2))
def _logloss(pred):
    p = np.clip(pred, 1e-6, 1 - 1e-6)
    return float(np.mean(y * np.log(p) + (1 - y) * np.log(1 - p)))

gof_rows = []
for name, m in [("Linear probability", lpm_full), ("Logit", logit_full), ("Probit", probit_full)]:
    pred = m.predict(share_df)
    r2 = 1 - np.sum((y - pred) ** 2) / np.sum((y - y.mean()) ** 2)
    gof_rows.append({
        "model": name,
        "r2": f"{r2:.3f}",
        "brier": f"{_brier(pred):.3f}",
        "pseudo_r2": f"{m.prsquared:.3f}" if hasattr(m, "prsquared") else "n.a.",
        "logloss": f"{_logloss(pred):.3f}",
    })

# Task 3 reveal — same hypothetical person, logit vs probit predicted probability
_mode_country = share_df["country"].mode().iloc[0]
_profile = pd.DataFrame({
    "smoking": [1], "ever_smoked": [1], "female": [1], "age": [55],
    "eduyears": [share_df["eduyears"].mean()], "income10": [share_df["income10"].mean()],
    "bmi": [share_df["bmi"].mean()], "exerc": [1], "country": [_mode_country],
})
_profile["country"] = _profile["country"].astype(share_df["country"].dtype)
logit_pred_profile = round(float(logit_full.predict(_profile).iloc[0]), 3)
probit_pred_profile = round(float(probit_full.predict(_profile).iloc[0]), 3)
profile_diff = round(abs(logit_pred_profile - probit_pred_profile), 3)

task3_output_text = (
    ">>> profile = pd.DataFrame({'smoking': [1], 'ever_smoked': [1], 'female': [1], 'age': [55],\n"
    "...                         'eduyears': [df.eduyears.mean()], 'income10': [df.income10.mean()],\n"
    "...                         'bmi': [df.bmi.mean()], 'exerc': [1], 'country': [df.country.mode()[0]]})\n"
    ">>> logit_model.predict(profile)\n"
    f"{logit_pred_profile}\n\n"
    ">>> probit_model.predict(profile)\n"
    f"{probit_pred_profile}"
)

# Task 4 reveal — Brier score computed by hand from logit's own predictions
logit_pred_full = logit_full.predict(share_df)
brier_logit_manual = round(float(np.mean((logit_pred_full - y) ** 2)), 3)
task4_output_text = (
    ">>> pred = logit_model.predict(df)\n"
    ">>> brier = np.mean((pred - df['stayshealthy']) ** 2)\n"
    f">>> round(brier, 3)\n{brier_logit_manual}"
)

# Calibration curve — real deciles of predicted probability vs actual outcome rate
share_df["pred_logit"] = logit_full.predict(share_df)
share_df["decile"] = pd.qcut(share_df["pred_logit"], 10, labels=False, duplicates="drop")
calib = share_df.groupby("decile").agg(pred=("pred_logit", "mean"), actual=("stayshealthy", "mean")).reset_index()
calibration_data = calib[["pred", "actual"]].round(4).to_dict(orient="records")

ojs_define(
    results_rows        = results_rows,
    results_n            = results_n,
    lpm_pred_min         = lpm_pred_min,
    lpm_pred_max         = lpm_pred_max,
    n_above_1            = n_above_1,
    uni_summary_text     = uni_summary_text,
    logit_summary_text   = logit_summary_text,
    ame_rows             = ame_rows,
    gof_rows             = gof_rows,
    calibration_data     = calibration_data,
    logit_pred_profile   = logit_pred_profile,
    probit_pred_profile  = probit_pred_profile,
    profile_diff         = profile_diff,
    task3_output_text    = task3_output_text,
    brier_logit_manual   = brier_logit_manual,
    task4_output_text    = task4_output_text,
)
```

## {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

::: {style="text-align: center; padding-top: 180px;"}
[**Binary outcomes**]{style="font-size: 2.2em; color: white;"}

[Every model so far has had a continuous y. What changes when the outcome is just yes or no?]{style="font-size: 1.1em; color: #aaa; padding-top: 20px; display: block;"}
:::

## Does smoking pose a health risk?

::: {.instructions-box}
**Business question**: among people who are currently healthy, does smoking meaningfully raise the chance their health declines over the next few years — once other differences between smokers and non-smokers are accounted for?
:::

::: {.fragment}
We have real data: 3,112 people aged 50–60, healthy at the start, tracked four years later. `stayshealthy` is 1 if still healthy, 0 if not.
:::

## The naive answer

**Naive answer:** compare the fraction of smokers who stayed healthy to the fraction of non-smokers who did. Done.

::: {.fragment}
**Why it's not that simple:** smokers and non-smokers differ in plenty of other ways — age, exercise, income, education — exactly the confounding problem from Week 6. And the outcome itself is different from anything we've modelled so far: it only ever takes the value 0 or 1.
:::

## What we need

- A regression framework built for a 0/1 outcome, not just a workaround bolted onto OLS
- A way to interpret coefficients when the outcome is a probability, not a quantity
- A sense of whether the model is actually any good, when it can never predict a 0 or a 1 exactly

---

## Binary outcomes and the latent variable

---

## What's different about a 0/1 y

- The expected value of a binary variable **is** a probability: $E[y] = P[y=1]$
- Frequency and probability become the same idea: 25% of cases having $y=1$ is the same statement as a 25% chance of the event
- So "modelling y" here really means **modelling a probability**

## Where does the 0/1 actually come from?

Think about what "staying healthy" really is — it isn't binary at all. Health is a continuum: some people are robustly healthy, some are fragile but not yet ill, some are already declining.

::: {.fragment}
There's an unobserved, continuous **latent variable** — call it $y^*$ — representing that underlying health trajectory. We don't observe $y^*$ directly. We only observe whether it crossed a threshold:

$$y = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } y^* > 0 \\ 0 & \text{if } y^* \le 0 \end{cases}$$
:::

## Why the latent variable matters

::: {.fragment}
If $y^*$ is linear in $x$ plus some random error — $y^* = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \dots + e$ — then:

$$P[y=1|x] = P[y^*>0|x] = P[e > -(\beta_0+\beta_1 x_1+\dots)]$$
:::

::: {.fragment}
This is a **probability**, so it has to come from the distribution of that error term $e$ — specifically, its cumulative distribution function.

- Assume $e$ is **logistic** → you get the **logit** model
- Assume $e$ is **normal** → you get the **probit** model
- Ignore this altogether and model $y$ directly with a straight line → you get the **linear probability model**
:::



## One family: the Generalized Linear Model

Every model this session share the same three-part structure:

1. A linear predictor: $\eta = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \dots$
2. A **link function** connecting $\eta$ to $E[y|x]$
3. A distributional assumption for $y$

::: {.fragment}
This is the **Generalized Linear Model (GLM)**. Logit and probit aren't a separate technique from what you already know — and neither, in a moment, will Poisson be.
:::

## The family, laid out

| Model | Link function | Distributional assumption |
|---|---|---|
| **OLS** | Identity | Gaussian (normal errors) |
| **LPM** | Identity | None — plain OLS applied to a 0/1 y |
| **Logit** | Logistic | Binomial |
| **Probit** | Normal CDF | Binomial |
| Poisson *(next session)* | Log | Poisson |
| Negative binomial *(next session)* | Log | Poisson + dispersion |

::: {.fragment}
OLS isn't outside this framework looking in — it's the special case where the link function does nothing at all.
:::

---

## The linear probability model

---

## LPM — the simplest option

$$y^P = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + \dots$$

- $y^P$ denotes $P[y=1|x_1,x_2,\dots]$
- Just OLS, with a binary y — everything from Weeks 4–6 still applies: logs, splines, interactions, robust SEs
- **Heteroskedasticity-robust SEs are essential** — LPM residuals are mechanically heteroskedastic

::: {.fragment}
Not just usually — **mechanically**: y is Bernoulli, so $Var[y\mid x] = y^P(1-y^P)$. The residual variance is a direct function of the predicted probability itself, which changes with x by construction. There is no version of this model where the residual spread is constant — homoskedasticity isn't just unlikely here, it's ruled out by what a binary variable *is*.
:::

## The bigger problem with LPM

We often want to use our model to predict outcomes. Let's do that here.

Predicted values - $\hat{y}^P$ - may cause problems.

```{.python}
lpm_pred = model.predict(df)
lpm_pred.describe()
```

```{ojs}
html`<div style="font-family:sans-serif;">
  <p>Predicted probabilities in this model range from <b>${lpm_pred_min}</b> to <b>${lpm_pred_max}</b>, across <b>${results_n}</b> observations.</p>
  <p><b>${n_above_1}</b> observation${n_above_1 === 1 ? '' : 's'} — out of ${results_n} — get${n_above_1 === 1 ? 's' : ''} a predicted probability above 1.</p>
</div>`
```

::: {.fragment}
One observation gets a predicted probability *above 1* — a meaningless value for something that's supposed to be a probability. Nothing in the LPM's structure stops this from happening.
:::

::: {.fragment}
For **inference** — uncovering patterns of association — this is rarely a big problem. For **prediction**, it's a real one: you can't tell a client their chance of an outcome is 104%.
:::

---

## Logit and probit

---

## Fixing the range problem

Recall the latent-variable story: $P[y=1|x]$ has to come from a genuine probability distribution's CDF — which is bounded between 0 and 1 by construction.

- **Logit**: assumes $e$ is logistic → link function is the logistic function $\Lambda(z) = \dfrac{\exp(z)}{1+\exp(z)}$
- **Probit**: assumes $e$ is normal → link function is $\Phi(z)$, the standard normal CDF
- Both are increasing, S-shaped, and strictly between 0 and 1

## Same data, three link functions

```{ojs}
Plot.plot({
  width: 640, height: 340,
  x: {label: "Linear index (z)"}, y: {label: "P(y=1)"},
  marks: [
    Plot.line(d3.range(-6,6.1,0.2).map(z => ({z, p: Math.max(0,Math.min(1,0.5+z/8)), series:"LPM"})), {x:"z",y:"p",stroke:"series"}),
    Plot.line(d3.range(-6,6.1,0.2).map(z => ({z, p: 1/(1+Math.exp(-z)), series:"Logit"})), {x:"z",y:"p",stroke:"series"}),
    Plot.line(d3.range(-6,6.1,0.2).map(z => ({z, p: jStat_norm_cdf(z), series:"Probit"})), {x:"z",y:"p",stroke:"series"})
  ],
  color: {legend: true}
})
```

```{ojs}
function jStat_norm_cdf(z) {
  return 0.5 * (1 + erf(z / Math.sqrt(2)));
}
function erf(x) {
  const sign = x < 0 ? -1 : 1;
  x = Math.abs(x);
  const a1=0.254829592,a2=-0.284496736,a3=1.421413741,a4=-1.453152027,a5=1.061405429,p=0.3275911;
  const t = 1/(1+p*x);
  const y = 1-((((a5*t+a4)*t+a3)*t+a2)*t+a1)*t*Math.exp(-x*x);
  return sign*y;
}
```

## Why raw coefficients stop working

- LPM's slope is constant — a one-unit change in $x$ shifts $y^P$ by the same amount everywhere
- Logit and probit's slope **changes** depending on where you are on the S-curve — steepest at $y^P=0.5$, flattest near 0 or 1
- Direct consequence: **you cannot read raw logit/probit coefficients the way you read an LPM or OLS coefficient**

## Marginal effects — the fix

The **average marginal effect (AME)** is the average, across everyone in the data, of how much $y^P$ changes for a one-unit change in $x$.

::: {.fragment}
- Computed via numerical derivatives, not by hand — that's what the `marginaleffects` package is for
- Has the **exact same interpretation as an LPM coefficient**
:::

```{.python}
import marginaleffects as me

logit_model = smf.logit("stayshealthy ~ smoking + ever_smoked + female + age + eduyears + income10 + bmi + exerc", data=df).fit()
ame = me.avg_slopes(logit_model)
```

---

## Is the model any good?

---

## Why R² doesn't quite work here

- A probability model will never predict exactly 0 or exactly 1 — so it can never "perfectly" fit a 0/1 outcome the way OLS can fit a continuous one
- $R^2$ can still be computed, but it no longer carries the same "share of variance explained" meaning
- We need measures built for probability outcomes

## Three purpose-built measures

- **Brier score** — mean squared distance between predicted probability and actual outcome. Smaller is better.
- **Pseudo R²** (McFadden's) — ratio of the model's log-likelihood to an intercept-only model's. Works for logit/probit, not LPM (no likelihood function there).
- **Log-loss** — a negative number; closer to zero is better.

## Goodness of fit, on real data

```{ojs}
{
  const cols = [["model","Model"],["r2","R²"],["brier","Brier"],["pseudo_r2","Pseudo R²"],["logloss","Log-loss"]];
  return html`<table style="margin:16px auto 0;font-family:sans-serif;font-size:1em;border-collapse:collapse;">
    <tr style="border-bottom:2px solid #1a1a2e;">${cols.map(c=>`<th style="padding:6px 20px;">${c[1]}</th>`).join('')}</tr>
    ${gof_rows.map(d => `<tr style="border-bottom:1px solid #ddd;">${cols.map(c=>`<td style="padding:5px 20px;text-align:${c[0]==='model'?'left':'center'};">${d[c[0]]}</td>`).join('')}</tr>`).join('')}
  </table>`
}
```

::: {.fragment}
Logit and probit edge out LPM on every measure, but the differences are small — consistent with what the marginal effects already told us.
:::

## Task — compute the Brier score yourself

::: {.instructions-box}
**Business question**: how would you check the table above wasn't just typed in?

The Brier score is nothing more than the same squared-error idea behind $R^2$ back in Week 4 — just applied to a probability instead of a price. Get logit's predicted probabilities with `.predict()`, then compute `np.mean((pred - y) ** 2)` by hand. Does it match the table? No further syntax hints.
:::

## What you should have found

```{ojs}
html`<pre style="font-family:'SF Mono','Menlo',monospace;font-size:0.62em;line-height:1.4;
                  background:#f6f6f8;border:1px solid #e0e0e6;border-radius:6px;
                  padding:8px 14px;overflow-x:auto;white-space:pre;">${task4_output_text}</pre>`
```

::: {.instructions-box}
Same number as the table — **${brier_logit_manual}**. Goodness of fit for a probability model isn't a mysterious new statistic, it's MSE wearing a different name.
:::

## Calibration — a sharper question

Unbiasedness asks: is the model right *on average*? Calibration asks something stricter: is it right at **every** predicted probability level?

::: {.fragment}
Take everyone predicted around a 30% chance of staying healthy. If roughly 30% of them actually did, the model is well calibrated there. Do this across the whole range of predictions — that's a **calibration curve**.
:::

## Real calibration curve

```{.python}
df["pred_logit"] = logit_model.predict(df)
df["decile"] = pd.qcut(df["pred_logit"], 10, labels=False)

calib = (df.groupby("decile")
           .agg(pred=("pred_logit", "mean"), actual=("stayshealthy", "mean"))
           .reset_index())
```

```{ojs}
Plot.plot({
  width: 500, height: 420,
  x: {label: "Predicted probability", domain: [0,1]},
  y: {label: "Actual outcome rate", domain: [0,1]},
  marks: [
    Plot.line([{x:0,y:0},{x:1,y:1}], {x:"x", y:"y", stroke:"#ccc", strokeDasharray:"4,4"}),
    Plot.line(calibration_data, {x:"pred", y:"actual", stroke:"#2d6a4f", strokeWidth:2}),
    Plot.dot(calibration_data, {x:"pred", y:"actual", fill:"#2d6a4f", r:4})
  ]
})
```

::: {.fragment}
Deciles of predicted probability from the logit model, against the actual fraction who stayed healthy in each decile. Close to the diagonal — well calibrated, not just unbiased on average.
:::

---

## Back to the question

---

## So, does smoking matter?

- Smokers are genuinely less likely to stay healthy — roughly **6–7 percentage points**, robust across LPM, logit, and probit, and it survives controlling for age, income, education, and exercise
- The model is reasonably well calibrated — its predicted probabilities can be trusted, not just its average direction
- LPM, logit, and probit tell essentially the same story here — a reminder that the fancier model isn't always the one that changes the answer

## Summary

- A binary y is really a probability to be modelled — the latent-variable story explains why link functions exist, not just that they do
- LPM is OLS with a 0/1 y — simple, but predicted probabilities can fall outside [0,1]
- Logit and probit fix the range problem, at the cost of needing marginal effects to interpret coefficients
- Goodness of fit for probability models means Brier score, pseudo-R², log-loss, and calibration — not $R^2$ alone
